reading.rtitle: One Line in a Credit Policy
paras: In 2019 a bank in Curitiba wrote a rule that everybody agreed with. Above ten thousand reais, a human had to review the case; below it, the model could decide alone. The line was clear, it was short, and for two years nobody argued about it.

Then sales asked for an exception. One large customer, one afternoon, one waiver signed by a director. That was allowed: only two people in the bank could sign a waiver, and one of them did. Nobody did anything wrong, and the customer paid on time.

The following month there were three waivers. The month after that, eleven. Nobody had changed the policy and nobody had to: the document still said ten thousand, and the team still complied with it on paper. But everyone had learned that above the threshold you did not really have to wait for a human. You had to make a phone call.

The audit found it in twenty minutes, which is what audits are for. The bank did not tighten the rule and it did not remove the waiver. It changed one line instead: from that quarter on, a waiver had to name the requirement it was skipping, and any requirement skipped ten times in a quarter had to be rewritten. The exceptions did not disappear. They became a signal that the policy was wrong, which is what an exception is supposed to be.
reading.source: A composite account of a Brazilian credit policy review, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how a bank chooses the right threshold for human review.
To show how a rule that nobody broke stopped working, and the single line that fixed it.
To argue that banks should never allow waivers.

listenings.text: Welcome, and let me give you section four in three minutes, because this is the part people get wrong. Above ten thousand reais, a human review is mandatory. The model cannot decide that case alone, and nobody can skip it, whatever the customer says. Below ten thousand, a second review is optional. I am going to say that again, because every year somebody hears it wrong. Optional. You do not have to ask for one. It is not forbidden, it is simply not necessary, and those two things are not the same. Only two people in the bank can sign a waiver, and both of them are in this room. And finally, the audit. It happens every six months and you do not get notice. In an audit, a decision without a written reason does not exist, no matter how good the decision was.

An exception is only an exception while it is rare. Grant it often enough and something quiet happens: people start planning around it. They stop asking whether they will get it and start assuming that they will, and after a while nobody even requests it, because everybody knows how the phone call goes. The rule is still in the document, and the document is still true, and the behaviour has moved a hundred metres away from it. My number is ten. If the same exception is granted ten times in a quarter, the policy is wrong. Not the people, the policy. Rewrite the line. And here is my test for anybody who owns a policy: they should be able to say out loud which of their rules are actually enforced and which ones are not, without opening the document. If they cannot, somebody else is deciding.
